title: The platform, not the model, runs the steps
statement: Let the platform, not the model, step a learner through each part of a problem in order, because a prompt alone didn't keep the model on track.
example: In a randomized crossover trial with undergraduates, structured AI tutoring built this way had a median post-test score of 4.5 against 3.5 for in-class active learning.
detail: The Grade 9 research brief read in full a randomized crossover trial in which structured AI tutoring beat in-class active learning for physics undergraduates, with median post-test scores of 4.5 against 3.5 and a median time of 49 minutes against 60. Among the design elements the trial lists, the platform, not the language model, stepped students through each part of a problem in order, because the system prompt alone did not keep it on track, and expert step-by-step solutions went into the prompt to keep explanations accurate. The brief notes that the Grade 9 design already works this way, with authored answer keys feeding the judge and the platform controlling the sequence.
against: The trial was with undergraduates only (`othello-course-renderer-draft/repo/docs/design/grade-9/research/learners-voice-guide.md`, line 177), and these are listed design elements, not features it tested one at a time.

evidence.quote: median post-test scores were 4.5 for the AI group versus 3.5 for active learning, more than double the gains (effect size about 0.73–1.3).
the platform, not the LLM, steps students through each part of a problem in order, because the system prompt alone did not keep it on track;
expert step-by-step solutions included in the prompt to keep explanations accurate;
Our current design already matches this: authored answer keys feed the judge, and the platform, not the LLM, controls the sequence.
